<section class="section" style="padding-top:56px"><div class="wrap"><div class="sec-title"><span class="eyebrow">STUDENTS</span><h2>How value-centered character education changed students</h2><p>Students who take value standards as their guide in life help, respect and care for one another, and live positively and vibrantly, each with their own gifts.</p></div><div class="after4"><div class="afc"><b>“Youngchan, you’re doing so well lately!”</b><span class="s">Understanding and forgiveness between friends</span><p>When Youngchan, who had drifted away from friends, tried hard to be considerate, the teacher asked the class for understanding and forgiveness. At recess, classmates were the first to pat Youngchan on the shoulder with praise, and everyone laughed together.</p><i>A child who lost friends through anger</i></div><div class="afc"><b>“I can’t control it on my own yet”</b><span class="s">The power to judge without being told</span><p>Jungwoo, who was often late because of gaming, agreed to hand in the phone for a week. Even after the promise ended, Jungwoo kept handing it in, and by the second semester could manage alone.</p><i>A child overly immersed in gaming</i></div><div class="afc"><b>“Teacher, I held back my anger today!”</b><span class="s">Changes in friendships and emotions</span><p>Mina, who came alone to the teacher almost every period, gradually began coming with friends and a brighter face, and grew into a child who held back anger and kept promises to a younger sibling.</p><i>A child dependent through lack of affection</i></div><div class="afc"><b>A child who brightened by helping others</b><span class="s">A life changed by the value of love</span><p>Onyu, a class president who had only taken care of their own work, began helping friends with cleaning after learning the value standard of love. A once-dark face that avoided eye contact brightened, and classmates nominated Onyu for a good-deed award and as a leader.</p><i>A once self-centered child</i></div></div></div></section><section class="section"><div class="wrap"><div class="sec-title"><span class="eyebrow">CLASSROOM CASES</span><h2>How questions and empathy changed classrooms</h2></div><article class="case"><div><h3>Honesty chosen with a red pencil</h3><p class="who">Case 1 · Jinsu, 4th grade</p><dl><dt>The situation</dt><dd>After the final exam, Jinsu brought an answer sheet claiming it had been marked wrong, but the answer, originally 1, had been changed to 4.</dd><dt>What the teacher did</dt><dd>The teacher talked with Jinsu quietly after the other students left. When Jinsu stayed silent, the teacher didn’t press, handed over a red pencil so Jinsu could mark the answer, and waited.</dd><dt>What changed</dt><dd>Jinsu crossed out the answer, choosing honesty, and left with a proud, bright face. It never happened again.</dd></dl></div><div class="dialog"><span class="t">The conversation</span><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Jinsu, mark it yourself. A circle if it’s right, a cross if it’s wrong. A score you get by cheating isn’t your real ability. I hope you make the brave choice that lets you stand tall.</p><p class="act">(A moment later, Jinsu brings back the answer sheet with a cross on it.)</p><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Thank you for choosing honesty. Being honest makes you feel proud and at ease, doesn’t it?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>(smiling brightly) Yes.</p></div></article><article class="case"><div><h3>A lie is a lie, even as a joke</h3><p class="who">Case 2 · Cheolsu, after a fight with a friend</p><dl><dt>The situation</dt><dd>Cheolsu told a lie as a joke. When Youngsu called Cheolsu a “liar,” a fight broke out, and Cheolsu blamed Youngsu.</dd><dt>What the teacher did</dt><dd>Instead of lecturing, the teacher used the Three-Step Questioning Method, following up with “Why isn’t it right?” and “Who would it hurt?”</dd><dt>What changed</dt><dd>Cheolsu realized that lying harms not only friends but also oneself, and decided what to do from now on.</dd></dl></div><div class="dialog"><span class="t">The conversation</span><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Cheolsu, is lying right, or not right?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>It’s not right.</p><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Why isn’t it right? Who would it hurt?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>Youngsu… and it’s not good for me either. It can start a fight.</p><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>So what would be good to do from now on?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>I shouldn’t lie, even as a joke.</p></div></article><article class="case"><div><h3>The real reason, heard by asking instead of scolding</h3><p class="who">Case 3 · Beomsu, 6th grade</p><dl><dt>The situation</dt><dd>Beomsu kept bringing a toy puppy and playing with it in class, even after being told for over a month not to. Asked why, Beomsu sat silent, head down, for 20 minutes.</dd><dt>What the teacher did</dt><dd>The teacher reflected on having asked like an interrogation, and made it clear the question came from real curiosity, not from wanting to scold.</dd><dt>What changed</dt><dd>Beomsu finally shared what was inside, promised to keep the toy in the bag during class, and brightened up.</dd></dl></div><div class="dialog"><span class="t">The conversation</span><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Beomsu, you usually don’t bring things you’re told not to, but you keep bringing this one. I’m not trying to scold you. I’m really curious.</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>This toy is like my little brother.</p><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Do you feel anxious without it?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>Yes.</p><p class="tc"><b>Teacher:</b>Then how about keeping it in your bag and not taking it out during class?</p><p class="st"><b>Student:</b>(face brightening) Okay!</p></div></article></div></section><section class="section"><div class="wrap"><div class="sec-title"><span class="eyebrow">TEACHER VOICES</span><h2>How teachers’ happy reflection changes classrooms</h2><p>What teachers said after the “Turtle Teacher” training.</p></div><div class="reviews"><figure class="rev" style="margin:0"><b>A chance to reflect on my words, and compost for children’s growth</b><p>When I first faced parent complaints and a child’s unexpected behavior, I was flustered. But as I worked through it calmly, as I had learned in the training, I could look back on my own words and actions. I realized that small greetings and attention are the compost that helps children grow.</p><span>— Elementary school teacher, trainee</span></figure><figure class="rev" style="margin:0"><b>The power of empathy: thinking once more before speaking</b><p>Talking with parents, I felt irritated at first and had complaints. But when I thought from their side, genuine concern grew in me. I learned that pausing to think before speaking matters most for empathy.</p><span>— Teacher, trainee</span></figure><figure class="rev" style="margin:0"><b>The joy of the first child changed by questions</b><p>Instead of teacher-centered discipline, I learned the questions students truly need to solve problems and grow in character, and came to know what real guidance is. I’ll never forget the joy of first changing a student with the Three-Step Questioning Method.</p><span>— Kim ○○, elementary school teacher</span></figure><figure class="rev" style="margin:0"><b>With a heart of helping and caring, not resentment</b><p>I learned that guidance must go beyond simple discipline and address root causes based on value standards. Instead of my old habit of resenting students, I now understand their side first, with a heart of helping and caring.</p><span>— Lee ○○, high school teacher</span></figure></div></div></section><section class="wrap"><div class="contact-band" id="contact">
